jsnvu6-e183235-d1e106.summary: Rubric for Question 1 of d.25: whether explicit faith is and always was necessary for salvation, referring to Aquinas.

jsnvu6-e183235-d1e119.summary: Argument that explicit faith is necessary: as explicit knowledge of the precepts is needed to avoid moral sins, explicit knowledge of the articles is needed to avoid error and heresy.
claims: Explicit knowledge of articles is needed to avoid heresy, as of precepts to avoid sin (objection)

jsnvu6-e183235-d1e143.summary: Second argument: denying the need for explicit faith would mean the lesser have implicit faith in the faith of the greater; but no one has implicit science in another's science, and if the lesser could rely on the greater, conforming to their errors would not be imputed to them, which is false.
claims: One cannot have implicit faith in another's faith (objection)
Implicit faith would excuse following superiors into error (objection)

jsnvu6-e183235-d1e166.summary: Argument for the opposite: the articles are explicated through Scripture, and knowing Scripture is not necessary for salvation, else few would be saved.
claims: Explicit faith is not necessary for salvation, as knowledge of Scripture is not

jsnvu6-e183235-d1e179.summary: Outline of the response: what is meant by implicit and explicit, then the principal question.

jsnvu6-e183235-d1e190.summary: Two senses of implicit: as an act is implicit in a power or habit, and as a particular is implicit in a universal (man in animal). So one believes implicitly when having the habit without acting, or when believing only in general without descending to specific articles; correspondingly, explicit faith is either faith issuing in act or faith descending to specific credibles like the Trinity and the Incarnation.
claims: Implicit faith is either unactualized habit or belief only in general
Explicit faith is either actualized faith or belief in specific articles

jsnvu6-e183235-d1e229.summary: In the first sense, explicit, actualized faith is and always was necessary for adults: infants without use of free will are saved by Christ's merit communicated in baptism, but adults must add their own merit (James 2), and all merit consists in act, while faith is necessary to please God (Heb. 11).
claims: Adults need actualized faith for salvation
Infants are saved by Christ's merit communicated in baptism
All merit consists in act

jsnvu6-e183235-d1e262.summary: In the second sense, wholly implicit faith never sufficed for adults; something must always be explicit, namely, in every state, that God rewards those who believe in him. Reason: no one can direct acts meritoriously toward an unknown end, and the end of merit is reward, known by believing God a rewarder. Authority: Heb. 11. This was necessary in every time, even before sin.
claims: Explicit belief that God rewards the good has always been necessary for salvation
One cannot direct acts meritoriously to an unknown end

jsnvu6-e183235-d1e301.summary: Further explicitness varies by state and time. Those to whom revelation was first made had to believe explicitly all that was revealed to them and nothing else, since refusing God is infidelity and the content was knowable only by revelation. Others fall into three grades. The highest, the pope and bishops, must know all articles explicitly and how to persuade the willing and defend against heretics, and so must know Scripture: as chief pastors they must feed, multiply, and defend the flock; the Church would otherwise be insufficiently instituted; and they must judge the subtlest matters of faith in council (Titus 1).
claims: Recipients of revelation had to believe explicitly all and only what was revealed to them
The pope and bishops must know all articles explicitly, with Scripture, to teach, persuade, and defend
Bishops judge the subtlest matters of faith in council

jsnvu6-e183235-d1e415.summary: The middle grade—simple curates, preachers, and doctors—must know the articles in their substance as their office requires, referring difficulties and heretical attacks to superiors. The lowest, the common people, need believe explicitly only what is handed down by their superiors and the Church's common rite; today no one is excused for ignorance of the Trinity, Incarnation, Resurrection, Ascension, and Judgment, given public liturgy, feasts, and preaching. One raised in the desert with nothing explicit must live well by natural law, and God would then reveal what is needed, directly, by an angel, or by a preacher.
claims: Curates and preachers must know the substance of the articles
The common people must believe what the Church's rite and teaching hand down
Nowadays none is excused for ignorance of the principal articles
God provides revelation to one who lives well by natural law

jsnvu6-e183235-d1e459.summary: Reply to the first argument: precepts and articles differ; the precepts belong to natural law, known by natural light, so ignorance does not excuse, whereas the articles exceed reason and are known only by revelation or teaching, so ignorance is wholly excusable if not one's fault. Such persons can avoid heresy by not accepting what they hear at once, but examining, asking others, and suspending assent—'he who believes quickly is light of heart'.
claims: Ignorance of natural-law precepts is not excusable, but non-culpable ignorance of articles is
One can avoid heresy by suspending assent and inquiring

jsnvu6-e183235-d1e490.summary: Reply to the second: science and faith differ. Science knows effects through causes in things, so no one has science implicitly in another's. Faith relies on divine authority, to which every believer assents at least generally, and some articles are explicit to the learned in Scripture; so the lesser, relying on the authority of superiors as superiors in the Church—which is divine authority ('he who hears you hears me', Luke 10)—have implicit faith in theirs. Hence the error of some superiors does not endanger the lesser, who rely not on personal faith but on the faith of the Church's rulers as such, which cannot fail in all, being governed by the Holy Spirit.
claims: Implicit faith in the faith of superiors is possible because faith rests on authority, unlike science
The lesser rely on the Church's rulers qua rulers, not on their personal faith
The Church's governing faith cannot fail in all, being ruled by the Spirit

jsnvu6-e183235.summary: Question 1 of d.25 asks whether explicit faith is and always was necessary for salvation. Durandus distinguishes two senses of implicit faith: a habit not issuing in act, and belief held only in general without specific articles. In the first sense, actualized faith has always been necessary for adults, who must add their own merit, which lies in acts, to Christ's; infants are saved by Christ's merit through baptism. In the second sense, wholly implicit faith never sufficed. In every state, even before sin, one had to believe explicitly that God rewards those who seek him, since merit cannot be directed toward an unknown end. Beyond this, explicitness varies by state. Recipients of revelation had to believe all and only what was revealed to them. The pope and bishops must know all the articles, together with Scripture, to teach, persuade, defend, and judge in council. Curates and preachers must know the substance of the articles. The common people must believe what the Church's rite and preaching hand down, and today none is excused for ignorance of the Trinity, Incarnation, Resurrection, Ascension, and Judgment. One raised in the wilderness who lives well by natural law will receive needed revelation. In the replies, ignorance of the articles, unlike ignorance of natural-law precepts, can be excused, and heresy can be avoided by suspending assent. Implicit faith in superiors is possible because faith rests on authority, and the Church's rulers qua rulers, guided by the Spirit, cannot all fail.
claims: Actualized faith is necessary for adult salvation
Explicit belief that God rewards the good was always necessary
The degree of explicit faith required depends on one's office in the Church
Pope and bishops must know all articles and Scripture; the common people the principal articles publicly taught
Implicit faith in the Church's rulers is possible because faith rests on divine authority mediated by the Church
